intro: In south Delhi a white lotus 70 meters across blooms in concrete and Greek marble. It is a Bahai House of Worship: no idols, no sermons, no priests, open to every religion on earth.
page_title: Lotus Temple: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body: The commission went to Fariborz Sahba, an Iranian architect, who began designing in 1976. His brief was unusual: make the building feel familiar to Indians without copying any existing Indian architectural school. His answer was the lotus, a flower sacred across Indian religions, built at a scale no flower ever reached. Structural engineers Flint & Neill worked out how to stand it up; the ECC Construction Group and Larsen & Toubro built it. Construction completed on 30 September 1986, the temple was inaugurated on 24 December 1986 and opened to the public on 1 January 1987.
sections.heading: A lotus in concrete and marble

sections.body: The temple is 27 free-standing marble-clad petals arranged in clusters of three to form nine sides, on a podium that lifts the flower above the plain. They stand in three ranks of nine: the first two ranks curve inward, embracing the inner dome, while the outer rank curves outward to form canopies over the nine entrances. Inside, a double-layered dome modelled on the innermost lotus bud spans the central hall: 54 concrete ribs with shells between, ringed by nine arches carrying the superstructure. The hall is 34 meters across and 33.6 meters high, seating 1,300. The whole composition is 70 meters in diameter and 34.27 meters high, its white marble quarried from Mount Penteli in Greece. Nine reflecting ponds ring the site, because the lotus grows in water.
sections.heading: Twenty-seven petals

sections.body: Like every Bahai House of Worship, the Lotus Temple is open to all regardless of religion, race or any other distinction. Bahai law runs the interior: only scriptures may be read or chanted, in any language; choirs may sing but no instruments may be played; no sermons may be preached and no rituals performed. There are no idols, no photographs, no pulpits and no altars. Sahba replaced the statues and carvings of a traditional Indian temple with his two fundamental ornaments, light and water: daylight falls through the oculus and the petal seams, and the ponds mirror the flower. For a few years after it opened, the temple drew more visitors than the Taj Mahal or the Eiffel Tower, and it remains among the most visited religious buildings in the world.
sections.heading: A temple with no idols

sections.body:
The Lotus Temple's fame was built in print and on drawing boards rather than on film sets. It has won numerous architectural awards and been featured in hundreds of newspaper and magazine articles on every continent, becoming the single most reproduced image of modern Indian architecture. The 1987 documentary Jewel in the Lotus tells the story of its construction: hundreds of workers from different races, countries and religions raising a tabernacle of peace and unity.

Unlike Mumbai's Gateway or Mysore's palace, the temple has no Bollywood biography and no Hollywood set piece. Its cultural footprint is architectural: it appears in textbooks, on postage stamps, in architecture school lectures and in just about every list of the world's most beautiful modern buildings. That is exactly what Sahba designed it to be: not a backdrop for stories, but the story itself, a flower that 4 million visitors a year come to stand inside of.
